title: Analysis of the Impact of Working Environment Factors on Employee's Health and Wellbeing; Workplace Lighting Design Evaluation and Improvement
central_proposition: Optimized workplace lighting, considering both visual and non-visual (circadian) effects, is crucial for mitigating negative health impacts (such as eye discomfort, headaches, and SAD symptoms) and enhancing employee well-being and productivity, especially in environments with shift work.

concept_definitions.name: Circadian rhythm
concept_definitions.definition: Internal process that regulates the sleep-wake cycle

concept_definitions.name: Social jet lag
concept_definitions.definition: A mismatch between circadian and societal (e.g., shift work, school) clocks

concept_definitions.name: Seasonal Affective Disorder (SAD)
concept_definitions.definition: A type of depression which occurs when you develop symptoms of depression during the darker winter months each year

concept_definitions.name: Non-visual effects of lighting
concept_definitions.definition: Biological effects of lighting are also called non-visual effects and are related to the human circadian photoreception

concept_definitions.name: Visual comfort
concept_definitions.definition: Perception of lighting depends on several aspects such as illuminance uniformity, luminance distributions, light color characteristics, and glare

concept_definitions.name: Optimized lighting
concept_definitions.definition: Good lighting solutions that deliver the right level of light at different times of the day

argument_structure: The paper argues that modern indoor lifestyles and artificial lighting disrupt natural circadian rhythms, leading to various health problems. It supports this by reviewing existing literature on the biological and psychological effects of light. An empirical survey then demonstrates correlations between specific working environment factors (age, visual task demand, lighting satisfaction, shift work) and self-reported health issues. This is followed by an empirical evaluation of a workshop's lighting, revealing deficiencies. Finally, the paper proposes an improved lighting design and offers guidelines, asserting that addressing lighting deficiencies based on circadian principles can enhance employee health and productivity.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The primary mechanism involves the disruption of the human circadian clock by inappropriate artificial lighting, particularly during night shifts. This disruption leads to hormonal imbalances (e.g., melatonin suppression, serotonin dysregulation), which manifest as sleep problems, eye strain, headaches, and mood disorders like SAD. Additionally, inadequate lighting directly causes visual discomfort and fatigue. Conversely, optimized lighting, especially dynamic lighting that mimics natural light cycles and minimizes blue light at night, supports circadian entrainment, improves hormonal balance, reduces visual strain, and thereby enhances overall health, well-being, and cognitive performance.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: Implementing dynamic, circadian-friendly lighting in workplaces, especially for shift workers, will lead to a measurable decrease in self-reported eye discomfort, headaches, eye fatigue, and SAD symptoms.

Objective physiological markers (e.g., cortisol levels, melatonin onset, sleep quality via actigraphy) will show improved circadian entrainment and reduced allostatic load in employees exposed to optimized lighting compared to those under conventional artificial lighting.
Employee satisfaction with lighting conditions will increase following the implementation of a lighting design that meets legislative requirements and considers non-visual biological effects.
Task performance and productivity will improve in workplaces where lighting conditions are optimized to support both visual comfort and circadian regulation.
bridge_warrants: The paper explicitly links its findings and recommendations to Circadian Biology (CB), emphasizing light's role in synchronizing the biological clock, affecting sleep-wake cycles and hormonal rhythms (melatonin, cortisol).

It connects to Neuromodulatory Systems (NM) by discussing how light intensity and color temperature influence stress response, melatonin suppression, and serotonin production, thereby impacting mood and arousal.

Implicitly, through the concept of 'optimized lighting' meeting 'human needs' and 'visual comfort,' the paper suggests a reduction in prediction error related to environmental conditions, aligning with Predictive Processing (PP).
The paper implicitly links to Attention Restoration Theory (ART) by connecting good lighting to improved concentration and reduced eye fatigue, which are outcomes of restorative environments.
Implicitly, lighting conditions contribute to rapid, implicit evaluations of comfort and safety, influencing overall well-being, which aligns with Dual-Process Evaluation (DP).
methodological_critiques: The results of the questionnaire survey are based on the subjective opinions and feelings of employees; therefore, further research in this area is needed to objectively confirm the results of the hypotheses.
model_structure: The paper references and adapts the 'Environmental comfort model adapted to workplace lighting' (Figure 1, p. 2) as a conceptual framework. This model illustrates how different aspects of lighting (e.g., adjustable lighting, dynamic changes, optimal color temperature, sufficient illuminance, absence of glare) contribute to occupant satisfaction and well-being, ranging from physical comfort to functional and psychological comfort.
limitations: The primary limitation acknowledged is the subjective nature of the survey data, necessitating future objective confirmation of the findings.

paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: In modern society, humans spend most of their time in the indoor environment (home, work, school...). This indoor lifestyle constantly poses challenges to our physical and mental health by affecting our hormone levels and circadian rhythm. This article deals with the possible connection between human and working environment factors and the emergence of health problems in connection with work. Using statistical methods, the dependence between the six characteristics (age, length of employment, visual demand of the work task, satisfaction with lighting conditions, and shift work) and occurrence of health-related problems and discomfort (i.e., eye discomfort, headache, eye fatigue, and seasonal affective disorder symptoms) was examined. The paper also deals with the evaluation of lighting conditions in the workshop using the lighting design software DIALux evo 9.2. Using this software, two lighting variants were modeled. The first simulated variant included lighting parameters according to the currently used luminaries and the second variant contained more efficient LED luminaries.
